extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in politics, history, and persuasive literary essays (early 20th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing clear, forceful argumentative essays about public affairs—emphasising precision of terms, grounding in facts, moral framing, and rhetorically effective examples. Suited to opinion/essay writing that addresses national character and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and agree the meaning of key words
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vital in a discussion that we should make sure we are going by meanings and not by mere words; it is necessary to settle what we propose to mean by the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before arguing, define how you'll use contested terms (example: 'barbarian'). You needn't settle etymology, but ensure opponents/readers understand the 'thing' you mean; concrete examples (soldier saying Mechlin/Malines) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with clear, simple facts before deeper interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are not the whole truth. But facts are facts, and in this case the facts are few and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with an objective factual narrative to establish the groundwork (Chesterton gives a compact sequence of events and even a mock diary of July dates). Use facts to show causality before moving to moral or spiritual explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples and analogies to illuminate argument
rubrics_metrics.description: One can almost prove them with plans and diagrams, as in Euclid; make a kind of comic calendar or diary to show logical outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ diagrams, mock-diaries, analogies (window/elephant, coal-hole, kitchen chopper) and comic devices to make abstract points vivid and test logical consequences by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between methods and aims when criticising systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Barbarism is not a matter of methods, but of aims; you may be superficially modern yet aim to destroy civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate technical sophistication with moral purpose. When analysing a polity or system, separate 'how' it operates from 'why' or 'to what end' it operates (methods vs. aims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish causation: enquire into origins and provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: We keep the peace in private life by asking for the facts of provocation, and the proper object of punishment. We do go into the dull details; we do enquire into the origins; we do emphatically enquire who it was that hit first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning blame or prescribing remedies, examine sequence and origin of events rather than offer purely abstract moralising. Use documented negotiations and timelines to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimentality; pursue analytic psychological distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In all these matters I would avoid sentiment. We must not lose our tempers at the mere cruelty of the thing; but pursue the strict psychological distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist merely emotional reactions to atrocities or wrongs; instead analyse the underlying attitudes, principles, or psychology that produce them. Use calm analysis to strengthen moral critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make precise, testable charges rather than vague accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the immediate logical and legal origin of the English interest there can be no rational debate... the facts which involved England. It is equally easy to state the first facts; the facts which involved Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base assertions on documented actions (treaties broken, ultimatums issued) and present them in a way that cannot be plausibly denied; avoid reliance on insinuation or rhetorical fog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the principle of reciprocity/mutuality as an analytical test
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another idea... the idea of reciprocity; or, in better English, of give and take. The Prussian appears to be quite intellectually incapable of this thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political or social behaviour by asking whether actors imagine themselves to be in the other's position; use mutuality as a litmus test for civilisation, fairness, or legitimacy in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and expose self-contradictory or opportunistic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: They were charmed... with the scientific discovery that it may often be convenient to make a promise; and yet curiously inconvenient to keep it... 'necessity' and honour was a scrap of paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal when doctrines depend on double standards (e.g., invoking rules when convenient and discarding them when not). Use quotations of opponents' own phrases to highlight inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify different senses of the same label rather than assuming a single meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the German calls the Russian barbarous, he presumably means imperfectly civilised... Now we, the French and English, do not mean this when we call the Prussians barbarians. It is quite different from the thing attributed to Russians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term is contested, map its multiple senses (negative vs. positive barbarian) and show how different uses imply different charges; this prevents equivocation and strengthens critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical contrast and paradox to reveal absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose we arrange it in the form of a kind of diary... How long is anybody expected to go on with that sort of game? ... It will be noted that this ultimate test applies in the same way to Servia as to Belgium and Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft hypothetical sequences, ironies, and paradoxes (e.g., mock timelines, comic calendars) to make the audience perceive the logical absurdity of opponents' positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame moral and historical claims in terms of universal human goods
rubrics_metrics.description: We fight for the trust and for the tryst; for fixed memories and the possible meeting of men; for all that makes life anything but an uncontrollable nightmare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground political persuasion in broadly shared values (promise, trust, reciprocity, honour) to give moral weight and emotional resonance to arguments without lapsing into mere propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony and comic elements judiciously to strengthen persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a kind of comic calendar... The comic irony, which never fails to follow on the attempt of the Prussian to be philosophic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce humour, irony, and comic framing to expose pretension or folly, but balance it with factual and moral seriousness so that satire clarifies rather than distracts.
